articleHeadline: Cholera, Pipes and Evidence: Doing Rigorous Water Research Inside a Complex
articleSummary: In South Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, a cholera-endemic urban water program underscores the need for rigorous, embedded operational research. Climate-driven shocks—floods, droughts, erratic rainfall—heighten unsafe water and diarrhoeal disease, making investments urgent but insufficient without efficient use of funds. Rather than separate research, authors embed evaluation within a large-scale infrastructure upgrade aimed at hundreds of thousands of residents, aligning questions with managers' decisions on prioritisation, affordable connections, and measurement of water quality and cholera incidence. They acknowledge formidable challenges: laboratory capacity and cold chains for water testing; strained surveillance; long project timelines versus short funding cycles; insecure settings and shifting neighbourhoods. Using mixed-methods—quantitative water quality, epidemiology, and qualitative insights from households and institutions—the team shows how multi-stakeholder partnerships can yield practical, policy-relevant evidence on reducing cholera risk and improving water at the point of use.

articleHeadline: Three forms of plague.
articleSummary: Plague (Yersinia pestis) in Vietnam presents in three forms—bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic. Bubonic plague, the most common form, follows a flea bite with sudden fever, chills, headache, fatigue, and swollen, painful lymph nodes (buboes); untreated, it can progress to septicemia or pneumonic disease. Septicemic plague involves bacteremia with high fever, chills, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and exhaustion; severe cases may bleed under the skin, cause tissue damage, shock, and extremity gangrene. Pneumonic plague is less common but most dangerous, causing acute fever, headache, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, and bloody sputum; it spreads via respiratory droplets and can kill within 18–24 hours if untreated. Vietnam’s Ministry of Health classifies plague as Group A (highly dangerous); surveillance and preventive measures—sanitation, rodent and flea control, and avoiding contact with ill or dead animals—are essential, as plague is not common in Vietnam.
